items.stem: Ingrid writes: "One mole of hydrogen has the same mass as one mole of oxygen." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: One mole contains the same number of particles, but masses differ: 2.0 g for H₂ and 32 g for O₂.
items.markingKey: One mole contains the same number of particles, but masses differ: 2.0 g for H₂ and 32 g for O₂. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A circular hatch of radius 0.15 m on a pressurised tank in Hanoi has a gauge pressure of 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa acting on it. Calculate the force on the hatch.
How many molecules are there in 1.0 g of nitrogen? (M = 28 g mol⁻¹)
Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "The mole is an unnecessary unit because we could simply count particles."
items.answer: The mole is a practical bridge between microscopic counts and measurable masses, so it remains essential.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: N is the fundamental quantity. Arguments against: the numbers involved (~10²³) are unwieldy; chemists measure masses, and molar mass converts directly; the mole links the atomic and macroscopic scales. Supported judgement: The mole is a practical bridge between microscopic counts and measurable masses, so it remains essential.

items.stem: Define the term "pressure".
items.answer: The normal force per unit area, p = F/A, measured in pascals (N m⁻²)

items.stem: Explain, in terms of molecules, how a gas exerts pressure on the walls of its container.
items.answer: Molecules collide with the walls and rebound, each undergoing a change of momentum; by Newton’s second and third laws the walls experience a force, and the total force per unit area is the pressure.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Molecules collide with the walls and rebound, each undergoing a change of momentum; by Newton’s second and third laws the walls experience a force, and the total force per unit area is the pressure. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between molar mass and the mass of one molecule.
items.answer: Molar mass is the mass of N_A particles (g mol⁻¹); the mass of one molecule is the molar mass divided by the Avogadro constant, typically about 10⁻²⁶ kg.
items.markingKey: Molar mass is the mass of N_A particles (g mol⁻¹); the mass of one molecule is the molar mass divided by the Avogadro constant, typically about 10⁻²⁶ kg. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Chloé and a classmate in Lisbon disagree about pressure, moles, Avogadro's constant and molar mass. Which statement is correct?
options: Ideal gases exist at room temperature.
Pressure is force per unit area, a scalar measured in Pa; the same force can produce very different pressures.
Increasing pressure always liquefies a gas.
items.answer: Pressure is force per unit area, a scalar measured in Pa; the same force can produce very different pressures.
items.markingKey: B. The other options are common misconceptions. Pressure is force per unit area, a scalar measured in Pa; the same force can produce very different pressures.

items.stem: Briefly explain why hydrogen escapes more easily from Earth’s atmosphere than nitrogen.
items.answer: At the same temperature molecules have the same mean KE, so lighter H₂ molecules have a much higher rms speed (√14 ≈ 3.7 times N₂), and a larger fraction exceed escape velocity.

items.stem:
This question is about kinetic model of an ideal gas and the link between temperature and mean kinetic energy.

(a) Calculate the rms speed of helium molecules (molar mass 4.0 g mol⁻¹) at 273 K. [3]

(b) Explain the difference between the microscopic description of a gas and the macroscopic description of a gas. [4]

(c) Outline one argument for and one against the statement: "The kinetic theory of gases is a triumph of the scientific method." [4]
items.answer: (a) 1300 m s⁻¹ (b) The macroscopic description uses measurable p, V, T and n (gas laws); the microscopic (kinetic) description explains them in terms of the speeds, masses and collisions of molecules. (c) It is a powerful example of a microscopic model explaining macroscopic laws, with well-understood limits (NOS: models and evidence).
items.markingKey: (a) [3 marks] m = 6.64 × 10⁻²⁷ kg (M1); c_rms = √(3k_BT/m) = 1300 m s⁻¹ (A1). (b) [4 marks] The macroscopic description uses measurable p, V, T and n (gas laws); the microscopic (kinetic) description explains them in terms of the speeds, masses and collisions of molecules. (c) [4 marks] For: it derives the empirical gas laws from simple assumptions; it predicts measurable quantities (speed of sound, diffusion rates, specific heats); supported by Brownian motion evidence. Against: early versions faced opposition when atoms were not directly observable; it fails for real gases near liquefaction and needs quantum corrections for heat capacities. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: It is a powerful example of a microscopic model explaining macroscopic laws, with well-understood limits (NOS: models and evidence).

items.stem: Using the van der Waals equation with a = 0.364 Pa m⁶ mol⁻² and b = 4.27 × 10⁻⁵ m³ mol⁻¹, calculate the pressure of 1.00 mol of CO₂ in 0.00100 m³ at 300 K.

The van der Waals equation is (p + an²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT. For CO₂, a = 0.364 Pa m⁶ mol⁻² and b = 4.27 × 10⁻⁵ m³ mol⁻¹. (a) Calculate the pressure of 1.00 mol of CO₂ in 1.00 × 10⁻³ m³ at 300 K using the ideal gas equation. (b) Calculate the pressure using the van der Waals equation. (c) Explain the physical meaning of a and b. (d) Comment on the percentage difference.
items.answer: (a) 2.49 × 10⁶ Pa; (b) p = RT/(V − b) − a/V² = 2.604 × 10⁶ − 0.364 × 10⁶ = 2.24 × 10⁶ Pa; (c) a accounts for intermolecular attractions, b for the finite volume of the molecules; (d) about 10 % lower – the ideal model is poor at this high density.

items.answer: (a) 2.52 × 10⁵ Pa (b) Friction and flexing heat the air in the tyre; at nearly constant volume p ∝ T, so the pressure increases. (c) It is adequate for many everyday calculations, but high-pressure or low-temperature applications require real-gas models.
